source.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
source.authors: Johannes von Oswald; Eyvind Niklasson; E. Randazzo; J. Sacramento; A. Mordvintsev; A. Zhmoginov; Max Vladymyrov

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports toy-regression results about attention copying and gradient-descent-like in-context learning, but it does not identify or test induction heads or the specific induction-head claims.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses induction heads and reports its own adjacent-token copying results, but does not test repeated-token induction behavior, previous-token-head composition, or token-index loss. Claims about induction heads from Olsson et al. are cited background, not this study's results. Generic toy-regression loss transitions are recorded only as findings that fit no version.
record.test_reason: This study trains small attention-only and related transformers on synthetic linear and sine regression tasks. It shows they implement gradient-descent-like in-context learning. It never identifies induction heads, tests [A][B]…[A]→[B] completion, measures previous-token-head composition, or measures token-index loss. Its Section 4 copying result (first layer depends on the adjacent token e_{j+1}) is a token-merging step for regression, not induction behaviour. The loss transitions in A.11 are seed-dependent regression-loss drops that the authors liken to grokking, not to induction-head formation. The parallels it draws to induction heads are argument, not measurement, so it does not test V3 or V6 either.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, with corrections. The authors conclude that trained linear self-attention-only transformers on regression tasks implement (or closely match) gradient descent and GD++ in their forward pass. Copying through softmax attention is a second crucial mechanism enabling this. They say this differs from induction-head copying, yet argue induction heads could be seen as a special case of in-context GD. They also say their copying result supports Olsson et al.'s claim that softmax layers easily learn to copy. The findings are restricted to small models and simple regression.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains attention-only and related toy transformers on synthetic regression tasks and analyzes their weights, predictions, and token sensitivities; it does not apply the original induction-head method to language-model repeated-token behavior.
record.method_sensitivity: The copying result uses softmax attention in the first layer; the authors report that linear attention did not train for that setup. Training-loss transitions vary by seed, and changing from one head to two mitigates the reported instability.

fits_no_version.finding: In a two-layer softmax-first-layer toy regression transformer with alternating x/y tokens, the first layer becomes sensitive to the next token (not others) before loss reaches one-step-GD level. The authors interpret this as copying that merges input and target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A first attention layer can learn to copy the adjacent target token so a later layer performs gradient-descent-like in-context regression.

fits_no_version.finding: A single-head regression layer shows seed-dependent long plateaus followed by sudden drops to the GD loss. Two heads remove this instability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss phase transitions in toy in-context regression depend on seed and head count.

record.problems: The evidence uses small models and synthetic regression tasks, not language-model induction-head tests. The paper does not identify induction heads or measure repeated-token completion or token-index loss. Some reported trajectories are presented in figures without numeric values; training behavior is seed-dependent in the single-head setup.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the paper's broader comparisons of GD and trained transformers: they concern regression-task optimization rather than the specific induction-head versions. Cited findings about induction heads were not recorded as this study's results.

untested.parts: No identification of induction heads, no previous-token-head composition, no [A][B]…[A]→[B] behaviour.
No measure of induction-head onset or token-index ICL, and no co-occurrence with a loss bump.
No measure of induction heads' share of in-context learning in large transformers.
No survey of induction heads across models, sizes, runs or modalities.
No test of how data or training setup affect induction-head formation.
Proposes GD-based ICL as an alternative mechanism but only in regression toy tasks. It does not measure induction heads' role in few-shot learning.
No analysis of sub-steps in induction-head formation.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses call is kept. The paper's statements about induction heads are interpretive and cite Olsson et al. They are not measurements of induction heads, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test induction heads, composition with a previous-token head, or the repeated-token [A][B] … [A] → [B] behavior.
Does not measure induction-head onset or token-index in-context learning, or whether either coincides with a training-loss bump.
Does not test whether induction heads carry most in-context learning in large transformers.
Does not survey induction behavior across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Does not test how training data or setup affect induction-head formation or persistence of induction-related in-context learning.
Does not compare induction heads with other mechanisms as carriers of few-shot task learning.
Does not analyze whether induction-head formation consists of multiple sub-steps or transitions.

rows.subject: two-layer self-attention circuit
rows.operation_detail: Measured the norm of the first layer output's partial derivative with respect to the following input token during training.

conditions.value: softmax; the authors state linear attention did not train in this setup

rows.measure: Norm of the partial derivative of first-layer output with respect to the next token; interpreted by the authors as dependence on that token.
rows.value: figure only; text states the first layer becomes notably dependent on the next token before performance reaches the one-step-GD level
rows.note: This is adjacent-token copying in a toy regression setup, not the repeated-token induction behavior or head composition named by V1.
rows.check: Link is correct. This is adjacent-token copying in the first layer of a regression toy model, not induction-head behaviour or composition. The value is figure-only.

rows.subject: two-layer self-attention circuit
rows.operation_detail: Measured the norm of the first layer output's partial derivative with respect to other input tokens during training.

conditions.value: softmax; the authors state linear attention did not train in this setup

rows.measure: Norm of the partial derivative of first-layer output with respect to other tokens, excluding the following token.
rows.value: figure only; text states the first layer stays independent of the other tokens before performance reaches the one-step-GD level
rows.note: The authors describe independence from other tokens as part of their evidence for copying the adjacent token.
rows.check: Link is correct. This is the control showing independence from non-adjacent tokens. It is figure-only.

rows.subject: single-headed self-attention layer
rows.operation_detail: Trained across 10 random seeds and observed training-loss trajectories.
rows.value: figure only; the text says some seeds have long initial periods of virtually no progress followed by a sudden drop to the desired GD loss
rows.note: This is a generic toy-regression training-loss transition; the paper does not associate it with induction-head formation or token-index in-context learning.
rows.check: Link is correct. This is a seed-dependent sudden loss drop to the GD loss in a single-head regression layer. The authors liken it to grokking, not induction-head formation, so it cannot bear on V2 or V7.

rows.subject: two-headed self-attention layer
rows.operation_detail: Trained with two attention heads and compared its training-loss behavior with the single-headed setup.
rows.measure: Training-loss convergence and seed-dependent training instability
rows.value: figure only; the text says two heads mitigate the seed-dependent training instability and yield fast, robust convergence to the GD loss
rows.note: This result concerns regression-task optimization, not induction-head formation.
rows.check: Link is correct. Two heads mitigate the seed-dependent instability. This concerns regression optimisation, not induction heads.
